pr.title: gh-139269: Fix unaligned memory access in JIT code patching functions
pr.body:
This PR fixes a series of misaligned memory access errors in the JIT engine that were causing segmentation faults when running tests with AddressSanitizer (ASan) and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (UBSan) enabled.

The unsafe direct pointer casts in `patch_32`, `patch_32r`, `patch_64`, and `patch_x86_64_32rx` have been replaced with `memcpy` to ensure safe, alignment-agnostic memory operations.

<!-- gh-issue-number: gh-139269 -->
* Issue: gh-139269
<!-- /gh-issue-number -->

files.patch:
@@ -0,0 +1 @@
+Fix undefined behavior when using unaligned store in JIT's ``patch_*`` functions.

review_comments.body: Don't we also have othre unaligned stores for AArch64?
Can we cast this to `uint64_t *` instead of `void *` to stress that we're using a uint64_t value here?

No, should not cast to `uint64_t*`. Using `void*` is the correct and safer approach.

Casting to `uint64_t*` can cause undefined behavior due to:
1.  **Strict Aliasing Rule:** Accessing an object through a pointer of an incompatible type can lead to incorrect optimizations by the compiler.
2.  **Alignment Issues:** If the source address (`value + 4`) is not aligned for a `uint64_t`, creating a `uint64_t*` can cause a crash or performance degradation on some CPU architectures.

The `memcpy` function is designed to work with `void*` to safely copy raw bytes, avoiding these issues.
I'm not well-versed enough here to be sure at first glance that this is correct. So I'd wait for Mark's input, or anyone else that can confirm this is correct.

This looks wrong to me.

@ashm-dev why did you make this change?
The release build was crashing with a segfault without this change. There’s a related issue linked in the PR, although it’s currently closed.

That doesn't explain why you made this change. It seems unrelated to the issue.
This change is incorrect: `LOAD_GLOBAL` doesn't introduce a dependency on the globals or builtins. A trace containing `LOAD_GLOBAL` remains valid if either are modified.

> Is there a specific spot in the AArch64 code you think I should look at

Not really, just that all aarch64-based functions use `set_bits` and this one isn't used on x86_64 so we should also have someone check it (I don't have such machines).

> FTR, AArch64 patches are only used for AArch64 so be sure to test this on the corresponding architecture as well (in the reported issue, I see that the architecture is x86_64, but I don't know if you have access to an Apple Darwin with ARM64). Note that `patch_32` is unused on an x86_64 architecture and is (I think) only used for Windows 32bit.

The Arm runners should cover Linux, Windows and macOS on Arm. They seem all to pass but also we are not running 

```
            --with-address-sanitizer \
            --with-undefined-behavior-sanitizer
```

with the JIT. Maybe we should have some coverage for that?

Besides I'm pondering the cost of introducing `memcpy` for all build as they will be frequently executed.

> Besides I'm pondering the cost of introducing `memcpy` for all build as they will be frequently executed.

I believe it is like a type punning and should be opmizied - https://blog.regehr.org/archives/959

> I believe it is like a type punning and should be opmizied

It depends on the optimization level. In `-O3`, alignment is essentially ignored and the assembly will look the same, whether you use memcpy or not, but that's with clang on `x86_64`. For ARM, the picture is different depending on the architecture. On ARMv7, the `memcpy` is expanded into

```asm
patch_32_memcpy:
        lsr     r1, r2, #24
        lsr     r3, r2, #16
        lsr     r12, r2, #8
        strb    r2, [r0]
        strb    r1, [r0, #3]
        strb    r3, [r0, #2]
        strb    r12, [r0, #1]
        bx      lr
```

On ARMv8, it's the same. I suggest playing with https://godbolt.org/z/zovMEW7Ta to see the differences.

Interestingly, adding `-march=armv7` produces
```
patch_32_memcpy:
        str     r2, [r0]
        bx      lr
```
I would have assumed that's the default on `armv7-a clang`.

FWIW, `ARM GCC (unknown eabi)` behaves the same (producing the fast version only with `-march=armv7`), but `ARM GCC (linux)` produces the fast version since 9.3.0, before it needs `-march=armv7`, too.
@picnixz Yes, you were right - `set_bits` was problematic as well. I’ve fixed everything.

> Interestingly, adding -march=armv7 produces

Are we doing it on our side by default? should we do it? (I don't know). Actually, I also don't know if it's possible to have the JIT on Windows with a non-clang compiler (like, do we have JIT support for Windows + MSVC? if so, `memcpy` is, AFAIR, an intrinsic and there is some `call` instruction, so I don't know if there is a possible penalty).
I had built it yesterday with `.\PCBuild\build.bat -p x64 --experimental-jit-interpreter` and it seems to work correct.

You might not even need to add `-march=armv7` if the compiler has the full context. On Godbolt, we're just comparing isolated functions, so the compiler, lacking that context, generates unoptimized assembly with all the safety checks.

> You might not even need to add -march=armv7 if the compiler has the full context

I would prefer to know for certainty that it is the case.

> I had built it yesterday with .\PCBuild\build.bat -p x64 --experimental-jit-interpreter and it seems to work correct.

Thanks. Is there a way to have UB sanitizer enabled as well? I know that there are still lots of other UBs on Windows builds so it would be good to know.
That wasn't what I meant. I meant: are we sure that most of the time it will be an aligned pointer here? or more precisely, are we sure the compiler will be able to optimize this like that?

> That wasn't what I meant. I meant: are we sure that most of the time it will be an aligned pointer here? or more precisely, are we sure the compiler will be able to optimize this like that?

I can’t guarantee that the compiler will always fold memcpy into a single store in 100% of cases. As an alternative, I suggest we de-prioritize ARMv7. It’s an aging architecture with a shrinking footprint; by the Python 3.15 timeline it’s likely to be niche. We should optimize for the dominant targets (AArch64 and x86_64) and avoid carrying extra complexity solely for ARMv7. If needed, we can keep a correct (potentially slightly slower) fallback on ARMv7 without blocking this change.

> I can’t guarantee that the compiler will always fold memcpy into a single store in 100% of cases

Well, my concern was more about Windows & MSVC which doesn't seem to optimize `memcpy` (or does it?) I agree that ARMv7 is quite niche, but MSVC is not.

See https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/3779f2b95ebf68e2d5f8ea27c7a7baa0879f5496/Tools/jit/_stencils.py#L61-L62
https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/3779f2b95ebf68e2d5f8ea27c7a7baa0879f5496/Tools/jit/_stencils.py#L68-L70

(I'm not entirely sure that this actually means that the patch functions will be compiled using MSVC by the way)

@picnixz 
> my concern was more about Windows & MSVC which doesn't seem to optimize memcpy (or does it?)

[Godbolt](https://godbolt.org/z/8nj4Gds99) shows that MSVC also optimizes memcpy when the `/O2` optimization flag is enabled.

P.S. The `/O2` flag is the MSVC counterpart to `-O3` in GCC/Clang.

> P.S. The /O2 flag is the MSVC counterpart to -O3 in GCC/Clang.

Oh, that's why what I did had no effect. I used -O3 :') Ok. So, all compilers and supported archs seem to be optimized properly, except when hints are not given sometimes but that's only on an old architecture.

On my side, I would say it's fine. However, I'd like to know the opinion of JIT experts and maybe some benchmarks as well to see if this is true in practice. JIT+PGO would suffice (LTO takes some time...).
And since we accept these changes, this [issue](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/139288) is already becoming relevant)

> And since we accept these changes, this https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/139288 is already becoming relevant)

Oh right, I forgot about this one. However, this is annoying then. Should we first care about fixing the possible tests before actually fixing this specific UB? Because if we merge this PR, then we will have `main` in an even less stable state IMO.

Do you have a fix for that issue in particular? Because I would prefer not fixing the UB here rather than having a real crash on ASAN.

> Do you have a fix for that issue in particular?

Yes, so far the description of the problem is in the form of a hypothesis, now I'm looking for options to fix it.

A preceding test in test_asyncio is corrupting some internal state (e.g., memory layout, an object's type, or internal JIT caches). This corruption does not cause an immediate crash but leads to a fatal error later when the JIT compiler attempts to process code during the "victim" test.

@picnixz The JIT optimizer had a memory leak because it wasn't tracking dependencies on global and builtin namespaces when encountering `LOAD_GLOBAL` opcodes. This caused cached executors to become stale without proper invalidation when globals were modified. The fix adds explicit dependency tracking by registering `frame->f_globals` and `frame->f_builtins` in the dependencies bloom filter, resolving memory leaks in release builds. The issue still persists in debug builds and I'm currently working on fixing that.

@picnixz 
You were right — the segfault is not related to my changes. Here’s how you can reproduce it in the main branch:

1. Build with the following script:

   ```bash
   #!/bin/bash
   set -e

   BUILD_DIR="build/debug"

   echo "--- Configuring and building in $BUILD_DIR ---"
   mkdir -p "$BUILD_DIR"
   cd "$BUILD_DIR"

   CC=clang CXX=clang++ ../../configure --with-pydebug \
       --with-address-sanitizer \
       --with-undefined-behavior-sanitizer \
       --enable-experimental-jit

   make -j$(nproc)

   echo "--- Build complete in $BUILD_DIR. Executable: $PWD/python ---"
   cd ../..
   ```

2. Run the tests with `python -m test`. They’ll likely fail with the same error I described in this [issue](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/139269).

3. Start the REPL with `python`.

4. Type `import ins` and then press `Tab` for autocompletion.

5. Voilà — you’ll get a very unexpected segfault. It doesn’t only happen here, but this is the simplest case to reproduce. It seems to be related to `inspect`.


So maybe you could consider merging my current changes and reopening my [issue](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/139288) related to this bug, since it appears to be the same underlying problem.
